newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia imports sail higher on capital jump.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia imports sail higher on capital jump.

text.p: Australia's import bill has risen to its second highest level on record, with the stronger than expected January figure boosted by the unexpected inclusion of a number of shipping vessels.
Merchandise imports rose 5.7 percent in January, boosted by the inclusion of a number of vessels worth A$145 million that saw the capital goods component post a hefty 29 percent rise.

Forecasts had centred on a 2.0 percent rise for the month. "I think we're probably going to have to abstract from some special factors in there," Bankers Trust Australia senior economist David Bassanese said.

The rise in capital goods more than countered falls of 0.7 percent and 0.8 percent in consumer and intermediate goods respectively, and took the imports bill to A$6.792 billion, second only to July 1995's record A$6.829 billion tab.
The strong rise in capital goods was welcomed because of the positive impact on employment, and economists said that while it was most likely a one-off rise, it was still investment.

"Obviously there's a lot of monthly volatility in these numbers, but that would be in line with the sort of thinking that's behind the government's forecasts," Merrill Lynch Australia chief economist Nigel Douglas said.

That forecast, of a 17 percent increase in business investment in 1996/97 (July-June) is seen as one of the key pillars of economic growth, and the monthly rise fitted in with expectations of a more bouyant economy in 1997.

"Overall, I think it's just another one of the indicators that we're going to get over early 1997 that'll add to the stock of stronger than expected numbers," HongKong Bank economist Anthony Thompson said.
The rise in capital goods took them to A$1.814 billion, their highest level since the series began.
The Bureau of Statistics confirmed that a number of vessels were included in the monthly imports bill, but declined to be more specific as to what type of ships were included.

Economists said that the fact it was unexpected, when they would normally be aware of such large items, was becuase the ships most likely to be in question had arrived in Australia late last year, but ownership had not changed and therefore they were not considered imports.
If the ownership had subsequently changed in January, then the ship would have been included in the monthly import bill, and may account for the unexpected jump.
The imports jump also suggested that Australia's new monthly balance of trade report, due March 3, would open with a deficit.

"This sort of figure would be consistent with a fairly marked deterioration in the balance of goods and services when those figures come out," Commonwealth Bank chief economist Bruce Freeland said, forecasting a deficit of around A$350-A$400 million for January.
The international trade in goods and services report is replacing the monthly current account report, due to the inadequacy of some components of the monthly deficit.
Current account data will still be released quarterly, and monthly imports data will still be released on an international trade basis around the middle of each month.
